doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Student initiative and learning jazz on his own at Kent
summary: Dobbins and friends built what they needed themselves, transcribing solos and running Saturday improvisation sessions.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well I often tell students now, I think that the greatest benefit is that, even actually when we went into the school before we even decided to try to develop this program, all the students that I could remember were my peers and my best friends at the time, we were so proactive — I guess maybe, I don’t know if any of it had to do with the general social activism that was happening at the time — it was the period of the Civil Rights struggle and the Vietnam war and all of that. But my friends and I, if there was something that we felt was really indispensible to have in the school, we didn’t wait around for somebody to do it for us, you know, we just started doing it ourselves. And even in terms of teaching and thinking about improvising and chord scale relationships and technical aspects of jazz playing, there were some of the guys in the band that didn’t really have any experience in improvising but they really loved the music and were willing to learn. So I think about my junior year there I had already done a lot of transcribing of solos by different instruments and different styles. I wasn’t into much early jazz at the time, I developed an appreciation for that after I came here and put together a jazz history course. But at least at that time I’d checked out a lot of things, at least from the bebop era up until what was going on at the time, which was Miles’ band with Ron Carter and Tony Williams and Herbie Hancock and all of that. And every Saturday for a couple of hours in the afternoon the guys in the band would come over to our apartment and we’d have a kind of informal improvisation thing. We’d check out some solos that I had transcribed and people had questions about well why did they play this here, you know, about thematic development and improvised solos and chord scale relationships and things like that.
So your education in jazz was mostly your own initiative?

When you got here you had to figure out how to put your knowledge into something that you could teach more than one-on-one too, in a classroom situation. That was sort of new ground at the time I would guess.
